title: Aman Mokhade: The 'Enthu Cutlet' Breaking Records In Indian Domestic Cricket | Cricket News - News18
text: Usually, when a promising men’s cricketer speaks about his Virat Kohli-MS Dhoni-Rohit Sharma story, it ends up becoming more about them. Their invaluable advice, their inspiring attitude, their unexpectedly down-to-earth demeanor and so on. Refreshingly, in the case of this year’s Vijay Hazare Trophy top run-scorer Aman Mokhade, his Kohli-Dhoni-Rohit story reveals a lot more about him. It was 2017, and the Indian caravan had landed at the Vidarbha Cricket Association stadium in Nagpur for the fifth ODI against Australia. A regular volunteer for the matches in his region, Mokhade was fed up of doing ball-boy duties, especially in Tests at a pitch where all nine fielders usually do close-in catching for spinners and the ball hardly goes to the boundary. This time, he wanted to be closer to the stars, so he decided to be innovative. “I wanted to meet them, but the coach said the team only needed bowlers in nets," Mokhade tells News18 CricketNext over the phone. “I said, ‘No, sir, please put me in as a bowler. I will bowl and just see their routine before a game, how they practice.’… I knew if I could get a chance as a net bowler, I would get to be around them for two to three days of practice. That’s what I did." If you have followed domestic cricket over the past year, you might know Mokhade as a technically superb batter, with a huge range of shots. But he’s also an off-spinner, a leg-spinner, a wicketkeeper and a self-proclaimed ‘enthu cutlet’. This is his story. ‘Tu batsman hi banega’ Growing up in Nagpur, Mokhade hardly stayed at home. Most of his time would be spent on the ground in front of his house, playing tennis-ball cricket with his father, Ravindra. Ravindra, who had once harbored the dream of becoming a professional cricketer himself, saw the spark and enrolled him in a cricket academy at around the age of 10. There, Mokhade met coach Nitin Kanade, who got him up to speed with the basics. “I wasn’t even familiar with the concept of pads," Mokhade recalls. “On the first day, I just took a bat and went because that’s what I used to do at the ground near my house. I was so excited to play that I did fielding for two hours. But my mind was on the nets nearby. At the end, I asked him, ‘Sir, I have a bat, can I bat too?’ He said, ‘You don’t have pads.’ So he arranged someone’s pads and gave them to me." Among the youngest kids in an academy, Mokhade’s first couple of years were about fast-bowling because he just wouldn’t get the opportunity to bat. As he learned about the red ball and developed natural swing, he even got a taste for it. “One day, I told my dad, ‘I will be a fast bowler’," Mokhade remembers. “He just said, ‘Do whatever you want, but you’ll be a batter one day. Tu batsman hi banega (You will become a batter).’" Ravindra was right. Mokhade’s coaches saw something in him in the early age-group years and made him the team captain. The added responsibility pushed him to work harder on batting and the coaches, impressed, gradually kept sending him higher up the order, where it became more than just a secondary skill. But that didn’t get the bowling-worm out of him. In his under-19 days, when the team didn’t have a spin all-rounder, Mokhade was asked to fill-in and so, of course, he did. “I’m kind of an enthu cutlet, I want to bowl, I want to bat, I want to do everything when I am on the field. Off-spin, leg-spin, I can do both… I’ve even done wicket-keeping in a match! Once, we were playing a three-day match and nothing was happening for the bowlers, so I asked our keeper if I could keep for a session. I did that too," he says, adding that he still considers himself a proper all-rounder. Which one of his many skills did he show to the Indian cricketers that day in 2017? “They wanted to face spinners only, so I bowled spin. Virat bhaiya… he was batting a lot against the side-arm. I was just watching from the side nets. Eventually, he came and faced a couple of balls and went off. The wicket wasn’t that good," Mokhade says with a laugh. Around this time, he had met Umesh Patwal, the VCA academy coach who was asked to train the 30 best under-16 and under-19 boys in the association. Patwal helped Mokhade grow and has been a constant in his journey since, with regular conversations about any batting issues and even occasional trips to his Mumbai academy. In recent years, he has also made a couple of expeditions to another academy in the city, led by Yashasvi Jaiswal’s coach Jwala Singh, whose setup is famous for being near-identical to senior cricket with open-net practice and match-like fields. “I feel I have been blessed to have a lot of coaches who helped me in different parts of my life," Mokhade says. Comeback Season Although it was Ravindra who got his career started, Mokhade says his mother, Manisha, has seen his vulnerable side during the typical highs and lows of a professional cricketer’s journey. As Ravindra would often be off working his private job, Manisha would put her own motherly anxiety aside to constantly motivate him. It was particularly needed in 2022 when, at the age of 21, consistency in age-group cricket got him an early call-up to Vidarbha’s T20 side, but his performances weren’t good enough to hold onto the spot. That led to all but an exile from Vidarbha’s starting 11 for the next three years, behind more experienced competitors, across formats. “I was fortunate to get that opportunity," Mokhade says in hindsight. “I learned what kind of players are at this level, the mentality, how they score runs, and what’s required to perform. I was still playing age-group cricket at that time, so I was able to implement those learnings when I went back. Even if I didn’t get a chance here, I tried to apply those things in U-25 cricket, how to take responsibility, how to finish games when you are the only batter left, how to play the big innings when you’re set, how to get a start and how to bat in different situations." Indeed, later that year, he was VCA’s top run-scorer in the Under-25 State A Trophy (List-A) with 396 runs in seven matches at an average of 96.25. He maintained the level over the next couple of years. Then, in the 2024 Col. CK Nayudu Trophy (red-ball), he scored 670 runs, including a double-century, at an average of 55.83, which earned him his place back before last year’s Ranji Trophy. It wasn’t smooth sailing again. The youngster was run out without facing a ball in his comeback innings against Andhra and hit a good half-century in the second essay. However, his performances dwindled in the next few games and he was dropped, resigned to the sidelines as Vidarbha lifted the title. Mokhade was fidgety — he knew he was in great nick but needed another chance to showcase it, anyhow. He stayed with the squad this time, though, and maintained both his form in practice games and his self-belief. Still, although Vidarbha has one of the friendliest team environments around — most of them are childhood friends — Mokhade knew no one would give up the competition. “I kept myself motivated. At the end of the day, you only have to look after everything," he says. Finally, the chance came this year when Karun Nair left Vidarbha and returned to Karnataka. The batting spot was up for grabs again and Mokhade wasn’t going to give it up this time. In the first leg of the 2025-26 Ranji Trophy season, he smashed 577 runs at 96.16, the fifth-best in the competition at the time. In the T20 Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy, he was Vidarbha’s joint-highest run-scorer with 206 runs at a strike-rate of 157.25. Everything dovetailed beautifully in the Vijay Hazare Trophy (VHT), the 50-over competition. Mokhade smashed 643 runs from the first eight innings as Vidarbha flew to the semi-final of a trophy that they had never won in their history. Their opponents were Karnataka, the team that beat them in last edition’s summit clash in January 2025. “We hadn’t won any trophies, but if you see the last four-five years, we were very close," Mokhade says about the jitters of trying to achieve something like that. “We were always playing semi-finals or quarter-finals. We even lost a few finals… That did hurt, but it also gave us confidence. We knew if we just managed to come together in the knockouts, we can easily win the trophy. We just had to put ourselves together and make it happen." It was he who made it happen. Karnataka scored 280, with Nair the top-scorer. It was an above-par total for a pace-friendly wicket, especially for a team with one of the best pace attacks in the country. “They had read the wicket well; since there wasn’t much for spinners, they played four fast bowlers, that too all the premium fast bowlers who are now in the IPL and the India ‘A’ side," Mokhade says. “Plus, they had the experience of Mayank Agarwal and Karun Nair in their side. I could see them guiding every bowler all the time. When I was batting, I could see Karun bhai adjusting the field according to my shots. He knew the areas where I hit the most." The ball was pinging around and Mokhade lost his opening partner for nine runs. “It was very motivating for me to see that they were against me and wanted me to get out. They had that hunger. I thought I must have something special that they are so keen on it! Plus, all the selectors were there for the big game." As the juices kicked in, the result was a masterful 138 off just 122 balls, with 12 fours and two sixes. It had some unbelievable offside play, starting with deft usage of pace plus direction and then a transition to power and aggression. It was more than good enough to knock out the holders and secure a place in the final. “Most of my runs have come in 300-plus chases where the team is banking on me heavily. That gets me going," he says. Vidarbha went on to win the title and Mokhade took with him something extraordinarily unique: he became the fastest Indian to score 1000 runs in List A cricket (16 innings), equalling the decades-old world record of South Africa legend Graeme Pollock. “When I go into a tournament, I always want to be the highest run-scorer and the champion," Mokhade says. “But actually doing and achieving it is something else. It’s a sea of emotions right now, but we have to stay humble. We have another goal ahead of us. That thought is keeping me grounded and us humble as a team. We’re not getting carried away with that, bhai jeet gaye, jeet gaye. We are still focused on the next one." Rising Action It has been a long season on the road. Mokhade last went home and ‘chilled with friends’ — his favourite thing outside of cricket — after the first leg of the Ranji Trophy for a couple of days, though he says it’s all part of his life now. “I haven’t met my mother in a long time, but from our conversations, I feel she is very happy," he says. The sacrifices have led to results. One of Mokhade’s USPs is his all-format brilliance, which he credits to his mental clarity and his determination to just put in some extra time in the nets before a format change and iron out any issues. As of January 25, he is the only player in the top-five run-scorers’ list for both the Ranji Trophy and the VHT. He can be only the third, after Vijay Bhardwaj (1998/99) and Mayank Agarwal (2017/18), to top both charts in the same season. But that’s far from his mind, for all his goals revolve around just one thing. “Since I started playing, I’ve had one constant goal in my mind: I have to play for India," he says. “So every long-term or mid-term goal revolves around that. I want to play for my country, wear that blue jersey… I don’t plan too much, like ‘I have to do this much.’ I just want to go into every game with the same intensity, contribute, and dominate."

Comeback Season Although it was Ravindra who got his career started, Mokhade says his mother, Manisha, has seen his vulnerable side during the typical highs and lows of a professional cricketer’s journey.
